name: Wassoulou Empire (Samori Touré)
summary: An empire built by the Mandinka leader Samori Touré, who fought French expansion for nearly 20 years with a modern army and moved his whole state east; he was captured in 1898.

knownFor.label: Scorched earth
knownFor.note: Moved the state east as France advanced.

location.value: Southwestern Mali and upper Guinea, with its capital at Bissandugu. Ivory Coast is not mentioned in the part of the page read.

terrain.value: Savanna plains and wooded hills of the upper Niger basin, with the Fouta Djallon highlands to the west.

climate.value: Tropical, with a rainy season from about May to October and a long dry season.

resources.value: Gold from the Buré and other fields, grain, cattle and horses, and iron worked by local blacksmiths.

disasters.value: Constant war devastated farmland; scorched-earth retreats in the 1890s caused famine and depopulation.

population.value: At its height the state had 62 cantons and 10 provinces and about 300,000 people; the page gives no area.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: From 1891 to 1894 Samori moved his army and many subjects east, away from French advances, toward the Kong region.

economicBase.value: Trade with coastal cities in ivory, wax, hides, rubber and gold; firearms came through Freetown; the internal slave trade was fed by war captives. Horses are not mentioned in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Traded gold, ivory and captives for rifles and horses, mainly through Freetown in British Sierra Leone.

wealth.value: A war economy: gold and the slave trade paid for imported rifles and horses to keep the army in the field.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A military state: “the Samorian army was the preeminent government institution”, with an infantry wing of sofa and a cavalry wing; Islam was codified as the state religion in 1884.

keyRulers.value: By 1878 Samori Touré had declared himself Faama (Emperor). Gouraud surprised his forces at Guelemou on 29 September 1898 and captured him without a fight. The body of the page gives no death date (a reference title gives 1830–1900).

succession.value: Power rested on Samori alone; there was no settled succession, and the state ended with his capture in 1898.

institutions.value: Provinces under governors, often relatives or trusted officers, and army units that raised troops and supplies.

stability.value: Always at war, against the French and neighbours such as Kenedougou, though Samori’s rule at home was firm.

eliteConflict.value: Few rivals to Samori, though some commanders and conquered chiefs defected to the French in the 1890s.

armyAndTech.value: Rifle infantry and cavalry; workshops for guns.

majorWars.value: Treaty of Kenieba Koura with France on 28 March 1886; the French took Kankan on 11 April 1891; Touré besieged Sikasso for 15 months and it fell on 1 May 1898.

territoryChange.value: Lost his western lands to France and moved east, conquering new territory around Kong (1894–97).

alliancesRivals.value: Samori sought British support in Sierra Leone, which was refused; he was a rival of Kenedougou and the Toucouleur state.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded, but blacksmiths learned to copy and repair European repeating rifles.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade for guns and horses with Sierra Leone, but closed to French and rival control.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths, rivers and messengers linked army camps, markets and provinces across the savanna.

religion.value: Islam was codified as the state religion in 1884 and animist practices were suppressed.

languageWriting.value: Mandinka (Maninka) was the main language; Arabic was used for religion and some correspondence.

artsArchitecture.value: Few remains survive; mosques and fortified towns (tata) were built of mud brick, and many were destroyed in war.

socialStructure.value: Samori and his family, army commanders and sofa soldiers, Muslim traders, farmers and captives.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to Samori, Islam and the Mandinka-speaking army rather than to a long-established state.

dailyLife.value: Farming households in villages grew millet, rice and yams, but were often called up for war or moved by force.

neighbours.value: French Soudan, the Toucouleur state, the Kenedougou kingdom at Sikasso, the Kong region and British Sierra Leone.

ideasReligions.value: Islam served as the state ideology; Samori took the title almami in 1884 to stress his religious leadership.

colonisation.value: Samori was captured by the French at Guélémou in 1898 and exiled to Gabon, where he died in 1900.

riseSignals.value: The state existed from roughly 1860 until 1898; by 1878 Samori Touré had declared himself Faama (emperor) with Bissandugu as his capital.

peakPeriod.value: The page calls the 15-month siege of Sikasso (begun in April; the year is not given in the part read) the empire’s high-water mark, after which it declined; this does not match the entry’s early 1880s.

declineSignals.value: Major French offensives from 1891 forced Samori to abandon his heartland and move east.

outcome.value: Captain Henri Gouraud captured Touré at Guelemou without a fight in 1898, and the page says the state ceased to exist with his capture.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
